messages.body_plain:
Hi rmx,
first I approved only one of your last three messages as they seem duplicates. As explained on our group main page, every user's first message to the group is moderated to prevent spam. From now on your messages should be published in a timely fashion. As to the specific question, without more code and more detail on what you are trying to do I am going to make an educated guess and say "both". You need to add explicit row information and you need to use it as key. So for instance if you represent your matrix as  records keyval(row, c(val1, val2)) and you want to do a transpose, the program would look like

mapreduce(input,
  map = function(row,vals) lapply(seq_along(v), function(i) keyval(i, list(col = k, val = v[i]))),
  reduce = function(row, vals) keyval(row, vals$val[order(vals$col)]),
  to.data.frame = T)

or something of that sort (I haven't even checked this is syntactically correct).
This is a bit of a demo code, speed won't be that great and  I think if you have such skinny matrices it will be a challenge to make it much more efficient.  If I were working on something like this, I would explore a submatrix representation (row.offset, col.offset, submatrix), where the position is in the submatrix can be translated into the larger matrix by summing the offset.  So the transpose becomes

mapreduce(input,
  map = function(k, submat) keyval(NULL, list(row.offset = submat$col.offset, col.offset = submat$row.offset, submatrix = t(submat$submatrix)))

Again sorry for the sketchy code. You see here that the transpose is a map-only job, no reduce part, which is a big performance advantage. Of course we are  not trying to do only transpose, but it is at least one vote for this representation. Plus we have control on the size of the submatrix, independent on how skinny or fat the data is. That means we have a much better chance of achieving a fast implementation, by leveraging vectorized operations in R such as t(). My next step would be to implement matrix multiplication and see how that looks and performs. I hope this helps

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
The input file name is needed for two cases (so far):
- Creating some form of a 'document term matrix' when I have multiple documents (with different names) in one folder, and I want to go over all of them and know which word came from which file
- I have a couple of different types of data that I need to work with, and the easiest way to figure out how to interpret a row of data is to know which file it came from. I know that in a perfect world I'd just change the way data is being saved, but my world isn't perfect.

The reason why I'd want to use some process ID is to convert data from a 'matrix' format (a comma separated file) to a triplet format (rowID, columnID, value). I need to generate some form of a unique rowID for examples such as the linear least squares regression in the tutorial on the Rhadoop wiki. In this case I just need unique rowIDs, not necessarily consecutive rowIDs, so a combination of mapperID and an ongoing row count can be used as a unique rowID.

I don't think I should worry too much about more than one mapper working on the same line of code, as long as hadoop makes sure that only the outputs from one such mappers actually goes on to be reduced. If I should worry about more than one output from the same row being processed by multiple possible mappers being passed on to the reduce phase, my worries would be too worrisome to handle: in such a case the basic word count example is prone to produce wrong results.

It would be interesting to find an alternative way to transform data from a comma-separated matrix-like form to a triplet from (rowID, columnID, value) without resorting to crude measures like mapper ID and an ongoing row counter - let me know if you have one.

-Saar

Every mapreduce call. How do you know it doesn't change between iterations (actually, it does!)? I am not squarely against controlling better what part of the environment is shuffled around and I understand it can be a costly operation when one is mixing and matching big memory type computations with map reduce computations, which in practice happens very often, as long as the default is everything because of the design principle of providing an illusion of locality or semantic equivalence with local, sequential computation. On the other hand, this is the toughest feature to implement of the whole package and I am not keen on planning big changes in it. There are objects that need to travel every time even if the user doesn't see them that would need to be specified one by one. This part of the code would be forever fragile to changes, since the list would have to be maintained. Whenever you write a line of code that needs to be modified in response to changes anywhere else in the code, you know you are not doing the right thing and you are increasing maintenance costs for the life of the software. A few of those and you have a software nightmare. I'd rather support an exclusion list, a list of entries to be excluded from the environment propagated to the cluster. That way if you forget one, there's only an efficiency cost to pay, not a correctness one. I am not sure how I'd implement that, but it seems a less fragile approach. Finally, when I hear that  a job is slow at around 2 mins I don't think this is the right use case for mapreduce. Just read Lipcon's mr tuning recommendation from the Hadoop Summit and he clearly says that if tasks take less than that, maybe the granularity is too small. If you told me that just having a big matrix in the env added 10 minutes to a job, then I would be more alarmed.

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
You are using Hadoop for 1.2 Gb of data. Wrong tool. There are applications of Hadoop to small data, like the computation of an approximation of Pi, but those are not the typical cases and require special tuning and techniques and make sense for huge clusters.
You are comparing memory and disk and complaining that the latter is slower. Know your hardware basics first. Read this paper: http://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=1563874 . A half hour pleasant read will give you the basic numbers.
You are using a single reducer because your only key is NULL. That means even if your cluster has 1000 machines (a detail that I didn't find in your message) and is properly configured (you apparently have no system analysis to report, like how many processes are running on how many nodes), you are using a single one. So all this work to use hadoop just to compute at disk rather than memory speed. Get your mapreduce basics first.
Rather than posting hundreds of redundant lines of console output, if you are comparing two programs, post  both programs. It could be that your first program is so optimized that I could have learned something.
my.first.sample is defined after you use it in mapreduce. So I don't know what is actually called there. Please make code snippets executable.
dfs.tempfile is not exported. Why are you using it without documentation?
Antonio

Some more details and context about the application I had in mind:

- The output is a nicely formatted csv file.

- In the mapper: creating an 'ERROR' key, and throw the non-parseable data as a value.
- In the reducer, choose how to treat 'real' keys Vs. 'ERROR' keys. Have one reducer for creating the real output file, and have an alternative reducer for collecting the data that could not be parsed.

I'd love to hear alternative ideas for doing that in a single pass on the data.

Thanks!

-Saar

messages.subject_clean: Getting text data out of hdfs after we worked on it using rmr
messages.body_plain:
I'm running some ETL process on big data that sits in hdfs, but the output is going to be something that's small enough to handle with other tools.
So I'm trying to figure out what would be an efficient way to get data out of hdfs when I'm done.

When playing with output formats, I created a small sample code that has very similar outputs to the ones created by my ETL process. You can probably skip reading the code, but in case it's relevant, here it is:

######################################################
##
## testing outputting data saved in R to a csv file
##  on hdfs
##
######################################################

######################################################
##
## preamble
##
######################################################

##
## packages
##
require(rmr)

## set local/hadoop backend
local <- FALSE

if (local) {

  rmr.options.set(backend = "local")

  dataDir <- "~/IO_tests"

} else {

  rmr.options.set(backend = "hadoop")

  dataDir <- "IO_test"

}

dataOutCsv <- file.path(dataDir, paste("IOtest_", round(as.numeric(Sys.time())), ".csv", sep=""))

######################################################
##
## get some data into hdfs
##
######################################################

csv.output.format.2 <- function(k, v) {

  paste(
    paste(as.character(unlist(k)), collapse=","),
    paste(as.character(unlist(v)), collapse = ","),
    sep = ",")

}

myIris <- iris
myIris$Species <- as.character(myIris$Species)
myData <- to.dfs(myIris)

myMapper <- function(k, v) {

  myKey <- c(v[["Species"]], runif(1))
  myValue <- c(v[["Sepal.Length"]], v[["Sepal.Width"]], v[["Petal.Length"]], v[["Petal.Width"]])

  return(keyval(myKey, myValue))

}

mapreduce(
  input = myData,
  output = dataOutCsv,
  map = myMapper,
  output.format= make.output.format(format = csv.output.format.2, mode = c("text")))

The tricky part is getting the output data out of hdfs and into a local environment, so I can continue to use it with other tools. I suspect the actual output I'll be using is bigger than what I can hold in memory, so from.dfs didn't seem like a good option...
The best I could come up with so far is copying the resulting data from hdfs using something like:
$ hadoop dfs -text /user/cloudera/IO_test/IOtest_1340820605.csv/part* > IOtest_1340820605.csv

which, if I understand correctly, will translate all the outputs from the process saved on hdfs into a single local comma separated file.

Is there a better way of getting the outputs out of hdfs?
My current data is small enough to fit in a single part-##### file - does anyone have any idea if this syntax will work once I get to bigger output files?

Thanks!

-Saar

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am not 100% sure what is going on here but I noticed that you specify make input format with only three arguments, but it's not a guarantee that the default for the third will work with any combination, and in particular having a mode of text and the default sequence file format is not tested and doesn't make a lot of sense to me. You may want to set that to NULL. I guess we could have a bit more logic in there that selects that default based on mode, it's a few lines of code but it is just not clear what cases to cover. The idea is that there is a easy version of make.output.format, with a string format argument, in your case that would be make.input.format("csv", sep = ",') and the advanced version with the three arguments, a function, a mode (text or binary) and a java class. The steps are as follows
your keyval pair -> R format function -> some output machinery that depends on the mode -> a java class to read the data back into hadoop.

Unfortunately the last  step is missing in the local implementation, as we don't have any java components there to execute the class. It is not a deal breaker, you can do almost anything without, but it's the biggest divergence between the two backends. I understand the frustration, but we can't let perfection get in the way of the good and the two backends are almost equivalent, with the notable exception of these IO classes that are simply ignored.

Now on why  the combiner breaks things. When you are using the default java class SequenceFileFormat or some such you are expected to generate typedbytes on the R side, not text. What I think is happening here is that if you do that in local mode, the java side is ignored so no problem. When you are using hadoop and the combiner is off, java doesn't understand a thing of what you are writing out but it doesn't matter because it doesn't have to read it back in. When you turn on the combiner, the data has to be read back in to go into the reduce phase and if java can't make the distinction between key and value, which it can't because you didn't use the typedbytes format, it will protest.

So in practice I suggest you use
make.output.format("csv", sep = ",")
just to see if it works with the combiner on. If that does, you may still want to  use your format because of speed (this has been improved in 1.3, but for now the csv reader and writer are pretty sluggish). In that case, just add the argument streaming.format = NULL which will tell streaming to revert to its default behavior, which is text format. If neither of this works, I suspect we may be looking at a streaming bug. I don't have your data so please give it a spin and let me know what you find. I am traveling so I may not be as responsive as I would like, sorry about that.

Antonio
